summary: This standards-track document defines two techniques to improve the scalability of RSVP-TE deployments: Refresh-Interval Independent RSVP and Per-Peer Flow Control. They reduce the processing cycles and handling needed as the number of LSPs grows. The aim is to help networks whose equipment struggles with many LSPs.

eli5.summary: A teacher who keeps checking on every student gets tired. This tells the students to check in less often so the teacher can handle a bigger class.

subtitle: Two add-ons for RSVP-TE that cut the work a router does to keep thousands of tunnels alive.

tldr.problem: Routers that signal RSVP-TE label switched paths (LSPs) can struggle as the number of LSPs grows, because keeping each LSP's state alive takes processing cycles.
tldr.mechanism: Refresh-Interval Independent RSVP (RI-RSVP) makes the refresh interval very large and relies on acknowledgements and Hello-based failure detection instead. Per-Peer Flow Control lets a busy router slow down a peer that stops acknowledging.
tldr.outcome: Both techniques are advertised with new bits in the CAPABILITY object and are backward compatible, so they can be deployed step by step. The RFC is a Proposed Standard.

today: RFC 8370 is a Proposed Standard published in May 2018. It has not been obsoleted or updated according to its metadata, and it builds on RFC 2961.

sections.title: The Scaling Problem
sections.content:
Networks that use RSVP-TE (RFC 3209) LSPs are meeting implementations that have a limited ability to support growth in the number of LSPs. The refresh overhead reduction tools in RFC 2961 help with most soft-state scaling concerns, but analysis of existing implementations (RFC 5439) indicates that beyond a certain scale the processing can still disrupt a Label Switching Router (LSR).

This document defines two techniques that cut the processing cycles needed to maintain LSP state: RI-RSVP, which removes RSVP's reliance on refreshes and refresh timeouts, and Per-Peer Flow Control, which lets a busy RSVP speaker apply back pressure to its peers. Each gets its own capability bit (RFC 5063). Per-Peer Flow Control requires RI-RSVP, and the RFC strongly recommends supporting both and enabling them by default.
sections.eli5: Routers that keep many tunnels open get overworked by constant check-ups. This document gives them two ways to do less busywork.

sections.title: Required Support for RFC 2961
sections.content:
Both techniques build on RFC 2961. An implementation MUST indicate support for Refresh Overhead Reduction, MUST accept any of its messages, and MUST initiate all of its mechanisms (including the SRefresh message) by default, though a configuration override should be offered. It MUST also support reliable delivery of Path/Resv and the matching Tear/Err messages, and MUST retransmit unacknowledged RSVP-TE messages using exponential backoff.

One rule is tightened. RFC 2961 said a node receiving a non-out-of-order message with a MESSAGE_ID object whose ACK_Desired flag is set SHOULD answer with a MESSAGE_ID_ACK. Here that becomes MUST. The RFC explains that this predictability is key to taking any action based on a missing ACK.
sections.eli5: Before, 'say you got my note' was a polite request. Now it is a rule, because the sender needs to know when someone does not answer.

sections.title: Refresh-Interval Independent RSVP
sections.content:
RSVP normally depends on periodic refreshes to keep neighbors in sync and on a refresh timeout to clean up stale state. RI-RSVP removes that dependence by raising the refresh interval to a large value. RFC 2961 and RFC 5439 had already noted that doing so loses functionality, so this document adds requirements to prevent that loss.

An RI-RSVP implementation MUST:

  • support everything in Section 2;
  • default the refresh interval (R) to tens of minutes, with 20 minutes RECOMMENDED;
  • use a separate shorter interval (uR), recommended at 30 seconds, for state tied to unacknowledged Path/Resv messages;
  • couple each LSP's state to the RSVP-TE signaling adjacency, so that if the adjacency fails the speaker acts as if all Path and Resv state learned over it has timed out;
  • detect adjacency failure with the Node-ID based Hello session (RFC 3209, RFC 4558), with a recommended node hello interval of 9 seconds;
  • advertise support in the CAPABILITY object in Hello messages.
sections.eli5: Instead of asking 'still there?' about every single toy every few seconds, you just watch the door. If the friend leaves, you know every toy they brought is gone.

sections.title: Per-Peer Flow Control
sections.content:
Per-Peer Flow Control gives an RSVP speaker a way to apply back pressure to peers and so reduce a large part of the RSVP-TE control message load. An implementation MUST support Section 2 and RI-RSVP, and MUST treat a lack of ACKs from a peer as a sign of that peer's control-plane congestion. When congestion is detected it MUST throttle RSVP-TE messages to the affected peer, on a per-peer basis. The RFC suggests a traffic-shaping mechanism that cuts the signaling packet rate in proportion to the number of outstanding ACKs, and raises it again as that number falls.

It also SHOULD use a Retry Limit (Rl) of 7 (RFC 2961 suggests 3), SHOULD prioritize Hello messages and messages carrying acknowledgements over other RSVP messages, and SHOULD prioritize Tear/Error messages over trigger Path/Resv messages (those that bring up new LSP state) sent to a congested peer.
sections.eli5: If a friend stops answering because they are swamped, you stop sending them new homework and let them finish the old stuff and the urgent notes first.

sections.title: Capability Bits and Compatibility
sections.content:
Support is advertised in the CAPABILITY object carried in Hello messages. RI-RSVP uses the I-bit (bit number 28, 0x0008) and Per-Peer Flow Control uses the F-bit (bit number 27, 0x0010). A node that sets either bit MUST also set the Refresh-Reduction-Capable bit in the common header of all RSVP-TE messages. If a peer sets a new bit without that header bit, the matching functionality MUST NOT be activated for that peer.

Neither technique may be activated with a peer that has not indicated support. Turning RI-RSVP off means falling back to the traditional smaller refresh interval of RFC 2205. For Per-Peer Flow Control, a peer that has not signaled support SHOULD NOT be assumed to always acknowledge a message that asks for an ACK. This is what makes incremental deployment possible.
sections.eli5: Two routers hold up name tags saying which tricks they know. They only use a trick when both tags show it.

sections.title: Recommended Defaults
sections.content:
Appendix A explains where the recommended numbers come from. The refresh interval R of 20 minutes lets the refresh timer be set randomly between 10 minutes (0.5R) and 30 minutes (1.5R), similar in scale to an IGP refresh interval.

RFC 3209 defines the hello timeout as 3.5 times the hello interval, so a 9 second hello interval gives a timeout of 31.5 seconds, near typical IGP hello timeouts. A Retry Limit of 7 gives a rapid retransmit phase of 31.5 seconds, matching that hello timeout. The 20 minute R cannot be used for state of unacknowledged Path/Resv messages, so the traditional 30 seconds is used for uR.
sections.eli5: The numbers are picked so the different timers agree with each other, like setting all the clocks in a house to ring at about the same moment.

sections.title: Security and IANA Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC states that it introduces no new security issues. The considerations of the original RSVP (RFC 2205), of RSVP-TE (RFC 3209) and of RFC 5920 remain relevant.

IANA assigned two bit flags in the Capability Object values subregistry: bit 28 (0x0008) for RI-RSVP Capable (I) and bit 27 (0x0010) for Per-Peer Flow-Control Capable (F).
sections.eli5: The new tricks do not open any new doors for bad guys, so the old safety rules still apply.
